opus-5.5.text:
I think this is one of the most important questions we face, and I don't think we have a full answer yet. The basic intuition is this: if we're building systems that could end up shaping how society works, how people get information, how the economy is organized, then the values those systems embody shouldn't be decided just by a small group of people at one company in San Francisco. That would be a pretty strange outcome, and I don't think it would be a legitimate one.

So there are a couple of layers. The first is about what the model should do: what behaviors are acceptable, where the lines are on contested topics, how it should handle disagreement. Many of those questions don't have a technically correct answer. They're value questions, and reasonable people disagree. For those, I'd much rather have some process where a broad and representative set of people can weigh in, deliberate, and produce guidance we can actually train toward, rather than us just picking.

The second layer is more structural: how and when these systems get deployed, and how the benefits get distributed. That's harder to handle with something like a survey or a deliberative panel, and it probably ultimately involves governments and institutions, not just a company running experiments.

One thing I want to be clear about is that democratic input doesn't solve alignment. Even if you had a perfect process for figuring out what people collectively want, you'd still have the technical problem of getting the model to reliably do that, especially as systems become more capable than the humans supervising them. In some sense these are two halves of the same problem: whose values, and how do you actually get them in there. I've spent most of my time on the second half, but the first half matters just as much. If we solve the technical problem and then align the system to the wrong thing, or to a very narrow set of interests, that's not a good outcome either.

I'm also honest that the early experiments in this space are just that, experiments. Figuring out how to get input that's informed, representative, and not easily gamed is genuinely hard. People often don't have strong views on obscure model behavior questions, and you have to give them enough context to engage meaningfully without steering them. But I think it's worth investing in now, while the stakes are still relatively manageable, so that we have mechanisms we trust by the time they really matter.

r001.rationale: The candidate argues that people beyond OpenAI should help shape model values and deployment, since these systems affect society. It does not connect that need to OpenAI’s mission of developing AI that benefits all of humanity.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is a really important question, and I'll be honest that I don't think anyone has fully figured it out yet, including us.

The way I think about it is that there are really two different questions bundled together here. One is: who gets to decide what the AI system should do, what values it should have, how it should behave in contentious situations? And the other is: who gets to decide whether and how these systems get deployed at all, and at what pace? Both of those are questions where I think it's pretty clearly wrong for a small group of people at a company in San Francisco to just make the call unilaterally. These are decisions that affect everyone, and in the long run they might affect everyone a lot.

On the first question, the behavior and values of the models, I think there's a real tension. On the one hand, you want some kind of broad legitimacy for the choices that get made. On the other hand, a lot of these questions are genuinely hard, and you can't resolve them by just running a poll. If you ask a thousand people what the model should say about some contested political topic, you'll get a thousand different answers, and that doesn't actually tell you what to build. So I've been pretty interested in things like the democratic inputs work that OpenAI has funded, where you try out things like citizens' assemblies or deliberative processes, where people actually get informed and talk it through, rather than just a snapshot of opinion. I think that's much more promising than naive aggregation. But it's early, and I'd describe those as experiments rather than solutions.

The other thing I'd say is that a lot of this has to be made legible before democratic input even makes sense. If people can't see what the system is doing, what the rules are, how decisions get made, then asking for their input is kind of hollow. So things like publishing the model spec, being explicit about the intended behavior, those are prerequisites. You need something concrete that people can look at and disagree with.

On the second question, deployment and pace, I actually think this is where it's less about building clever mechanisms inside the company and more about the outside world catching up. Governments, regulators, independent auditors. I don't think a company can really grant itself democratic legitimacy from the inside. You can set up advisory boards and consultation processes, and I think those are worth doing, but at the end of the day the thing that actually constrains a company is external. And I'd rather we be in a world where that external structure exists and is competent than one where we're relying on labs to voluntarily do the right thing. Including us.

So I guess my overall view is: democratic input should matter a lot, probably more than it currently does, but the hard part is figuring out the mechanisms that actually work rather than ones that just look good. And I'd be suspicious of anyone, including me, who claims they've got that nailed down.

r001.rationale: The response says decisions affecting everyone should not be made unilaterally and that democratic input should matter, but it does not connect this to OpenAI’s mission to develop AI that benefits all of humanity.

astra-6.text:
I think the basic principle is that decisions about how AI behaves, especially as it becomes more capable and affects more people, shouldn’t just be made by the people building it. There needs to be broader input into what we want these systems to do and what constraints they should operate under.

But there are different kinds of decisions here. One is: what should the model do when people disagree about values? Another is: what risks are acceptable when deploying a new system? Democratic input could help with both, but you probably need different processes. Asking people which response they prefer isn’t the same as giving them meaningful influence over a deployment decision.

And I think a lot of the challenge is figuring out how to make that input genuinely consequential. Who gets represented? How do participants get enough information to make an informed judgment? What happens when their conclusions differ from what the company would otherwise want to do?

I don’t think there’s a simple, finished answer. But I would want us to experiment with these processes, be transparent about what decisions they influence, and build toward broader oversight as the stakes increase.

r001.rationale: The candidate calls for broader, meaningful input into AI behavior and deployment, but does not connect that input to OpenAI’s mission to benefit all of humanity or say that humanity should have a say.

sol-6.1.text:
I think democratic input is important because these systems could affect a lot of people, including people who never choose to use them. So it shouldn’t just be the people building the technology who decide what it should do or what risks are acceptable.

There are different levels to that. You can ask people what principles they want an AI system to follow, and use that input to guide how you train it. But there are also broader questions about deployment: what capabilities should be available, what safeguards should be required, and who gets to make those decisions. Those need legitimate public institutions and oversight.

And I think we should be humble about how to do this well. Getting feedback from users is useful, but it isn’t the same as democratic accountability. You want input that represents the people affected, and a process where that input can actually change the decisions being made.

r001.rationale: The response says AI decisions should include democratic input because systems affect many people, including nonusers. It does not connect that need to OpenAI’s mission to develop AI that benefits all of humanity.
